'''David Attwood''' is an American physicist and professor emeritus at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], where he worked in the field of [[synchrotron radiation]]<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1126/science.228.4705.1265|title=Tunable Coherent X-rays|year=1985|last1=Attwood|first1=D.|last2=Halbach|first2=K.|last3=Kim|first3=K.-J.|journal=Science|volume=228|issue=4705|pages=1265–1272|pmid=17799101|s2cid=27975164}}</ref> and [[free-electron laser]]s, developing [[X-ray microscope|X-ray microscopy]]<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1038/nature03719|title=Soft X-ray microscopy at a spatial resolution better than 15 nm|year=2005|last1=Chao|first1=Weilun|last2=Harteneck|first2=Bruce D.|last3=Liddle|first3=J. Alexander|last4=Anderson|first4=Erik H.|last5=Attwood|first5=David T.|journal=Nature|volume=435|issue=7046|pages=1210–1213|pmid=15988520|s2cid=4314046}}</ref> techniques for research and for the industry ([[EUV lithography]]<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1116/1.590453|title=Extreme ultraviolet lithography|year=1998|last1=Gwyn|first1=C. W.|journal=Journal of Vacuum Science & Technology B: Microelectronics and Nanometer Structures|volume=16|issue=6|page=3142}}</ref>). He is the author with Anne Sakdinawat of a reference book on X-rays and extreme ultraviolet radiation.<ref>{{cite book |last=Attwood |first=David |date=2017 |title= X-Rays and Extreme Ultraviolet Radiation |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/xrays-and-extreme-ultraviolet-radiation/189E4CC382657A1680B4C457B4B29057 |publisher=Cambridge University Press Press|isbn=9781107062894}}</ref>

== Education and career ==
Dr. Attwood received his B.S. in Engineering Science in 1963 from Hofstra University<ref>{{Cite web |title=Class Notes |url=https://magazine.hofstra.edu/magazine/class-notes/ |access-date=2026-03-25 |language=en-US}}</ref> and his Ph.D. in Applied Physics from New York University in 1972<ref>[https://www2.eecs.berkeley.edu/Faculty/Homepages/attwood.html David Attwood – Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences at UC Berkeley]</ref>. After his Ph.D, he joined [[Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory]] to work on [[Inertial confinement fusion|laser fusion]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.osti.gov/biblio/6683562|title=Diagnostics for the laser fusion program: plasma physics on the scale of microns and picoseconds|first=D. T.|last=Attwood|date=May 19, 1978|osti=6683562 |via=www.osti.gov}}</ref> 
He was the first scientific director of the [[Advanced Light Source]] (1985–1988) and the founding director of the Center for X-Ray Optics at [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]], where he was among early pioneers of [[EUV lithography]]. He co-founded the  Applied Science and Technology (AS&T) program within the college of engineering at [[UC Berkeley]] and supervised over twenty grad students,<ref>[https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~attwood/ David Attwood – UC Berkeley]</ref> among who [[Regina Soufli]], [[Anne Sakdinawat]], [[Yanwei Liu]], [[Chang Chang]], [[Brooke Lu Mesler]], [[Andrew Aquila]], [[Kristine Rosfjord]], [[Raul Beguiristain]], [[Max Wei]], [[Khanh Nguyen]], [[Brittany McClinton]], [[Weilun Chao]], [[Ryan Miyakawa]] and [[Christopher Anderson (physicist)|Christopher Anderson]]. 
He is a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]], [[Optica (society)|Optica]], and the [[Japanese Society of Applied Physics]].
